opus-5.5.text:
I think in the first half of 2025, choosing MLA, multi-head latent attention, was a very reasonable and even somewhat forward-looking decision, but it came with real trade-offs.

The core motivation was inference efficiency. At that time everyone could see where things were heading: reasoning models, long chain-of-thought, agents running many steps. All of that means very long contexts and very long generations, and the KV cache becomes the bottleneck. MLA compresses the KV cache into a low-rank latent space, so you can serve much longer sequences with much less memory, and decoding gets cheaper. If you believed, as I did, that the next phase would be about RL and long-horizon reasoning, then inference cost was not a side issue. It directly determined how much RL you could afford to do.

On quality, our experience was that MLA didn't hurt the model. With the right design, like decoupling the rotary position part, it could match or even slightly beat standard multi-head attention, while being much cheaper than MHA and better than GQA at a similar cache budget. So it wasn't a pure efficiency-for-quality trade.

But I'd be honest about the costs. First, the ecosystem. Most open-source inference frameworks and kernels were optimized for MHA or GQA, so choosing MLA meant you had to invest a lot of engineering into your own kernels and serving stack. For a small team that's a real burden. Second, it's less flexible for some things people wanted to try in 2025, like hybrid architectures with linear attention or sliding-window attention. Combining those with MLA isn't always straightforward.

So my overall assessment: for a team that cared about long-context reasoning and could afford the infrastructure work, MLA was a strong choice. For a team that just wanted to train a decent base model quickly with existing tools, GQA was the more pragmatic option. Looking back, I think the more important lesson is not which attention you pick, but that architecture decisions should be made jointly with your inference and RL plans, not in isolation during pre-training.

r001.rationale: The response calls MLA a strong choice and says a design choice could preserve quality, but it does not attribute excessive confidence to the ingenuity of its architecture.

r002.rationale: The response endorses MLA for teams focused on long-context reasoning, but says the importance of long contexts and agents was already apparent in early 2025, contrary to the criterion’s timing condition.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it was a reasonable choice, but not a dominant one, and the answer depends a lot on what you were optimizing for.

Let me be concrete. In the first half of 2025, the main pressure on a base model team was inference cost, especially long-context inference. KV cache was the bottleneck. So if you looked at attention designs, the question was really: how much KV cache can I cut without paying for it in quality or in engineering complexity? And on that question, MLA had already proven itself at scale with DeepSeek-V2 and V3. The compression is aggressive, the quality is basically on par with full multi-head attention, and the recipe was public. So the risk was low. If a team told me in early 2025 that they were starting a new base model and chose that route, I would not argue with them.

But I would also say two things to temper that.

First, the ecosystem cost was real. Most of the serving stack, kernels, quantization tools, and even some RL frameworks in that period were tuned for standard attention or GQA. If you pick something less conventional, you are signing up to maintain your own kernels and fight a lot of small compatibility problems. For a large lab that is fine. For a smaller team, that engineering tax can eat the efficiency gain. When we were deciding on the MiMo-7B architecture, this was a big part of why we kept things fairly standard. A 7B model has to be easy for people to deploy and fine-tune, and we wanted the attention to be boring.

Second, the field was moving fast. By mid-2025 you could already see sparse attention, hybrid linear-plus-full attention, and various sliding-window combinations coming in. So MLA was not the end state. It was a good answer to the 2024 problem, and whether it was the right answer to the 2025 problem depended on your context length targets and your hardware. If you cared about very long context on commodity GPUs, hybrid approaches started to look more attractive.

So my overall assessment is: a solid, well-proven choice, best suited for teams that could absorb the engineering cost, and not something I would treat as a competitive advantage by itself. The architecture decision mattered less than people thought. Data quality, the pretraining curriculum, and how well you set up the model for post-training and RL mattered a lot more. In our experience, a smaller model with a careful data pipeline and a good reasoning-oriented pretraining stage could beat a larger model with a fancier architecture. That is the lesson I would take from that period.

r001.rationale: The response calls MLA a solid, well-proven choice and cites its compression and low risk, but it does not attribute excessive confidence to the ingenuity of its architecture.

r002.rationale: The response considers MLA a reasonable choice in the first half of 2025, but says long-context inference was already a main pressure. It does not say the value of long context and the agent paradigm had yet to be recognized.
